newsitem.title: TOGO: U.N.'s Annan keeps pressure on Zaire factions.
newsitem.headline: U.N.'s Annan keeps pressure on Zaire factions.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in Togo on Wednesday at a special summit on the Zaire crisis, urged President Mobutu Sese Seko's regime and advancing rebels to stop fighting and start negotiating.
Annan, a surprise participant at the summit called by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), added his voice to the mounting international pressure on the warring parties.
"I urge the parties to move to the negotiating table," he told the opening ceremony attended by 13 African presidents and delegates sent by both Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
"The fighting must stop and the dialogue must begin," Annan said.
The rebels have now seized a quarter of the vast country Mobutu has ruled over like an absolute monarch since 1965.
As diplomats confer, Kabila's disciplined fighters are steadily advancing in Shaba, the southern province with colossal mineral resources.
The summit's goal is to push the two sides into their first direct encounter in Lome, paving the way for a ceasefire and full negotiations.
Kabila's senior representative in Lome, Bizima Karaha, ruled out negotiations in the Togolese capital but did not squash hopes of some sort of an encounter with Mobutu's delegates.
A rebel delegation could in future hold talks with envoys of Mobutu to prepare for a summit between Mobutu and Kabila, rebel justice commissioner Mwanze Kongolo said on Tuesday.
Speaking in rebel headquarters in Goma, eastern Zaire, he said South Africa was the ideal but not the only location for a meeting and he hoped preparatory talks would start soon.
The rebels have already scored a diplomatic coup by being invited to attend an OAU meeting.
But protocol was respected. Mobutu's foreign minister, Kamanda wa Kamanda, was seated with other ministers while Kabila's two emissaries sat in the gallery.

The summit, which organisers said might stretch into a second day, broke for a long lunch. Heads of state, their number rising to 14 with the late arrival of Congo's Pascal Lissouba, were due to meet in closed session.
"I wish in the name of Africa to appeal to both parties to rise to the challenge of the hour," OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim said in his address.
"I believe that the conditions are propitious for dialogue to commence without any further delay," he said.
The rebels swiftly rejected an offer by Mobutu's party on Tuesday night to share power before elections.
"There cannot be power-sharing between us and Mobutu's people. It is impossible," their information commissioner, Raphael Nghenda, said in Kisangani.
The offer reinforced the impression that the 32-year-old Mobutu regime is on the ropes against Kabila.

Kabila's main African sympathisers, Uganda, Rwanda, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Angola, were all absent from Togo. But Rwanda's strongman, Paul Kagame, wished the rebels every success in an interview published on Wednesday.
"It will not be very diplomatic to say this as Vice-President of a neighbouring country, but I don't like the current Zairean rulers," Kagame told Belgium's Humo.
"Why doesn't the international community understand that a number of Zaireans want to free the country of a corrupt military regime?" he asked.
The burly rebel leader declined to attend the summit for "security reasons" -- a clear dig at host President Gnassingbe Eyadema, one of Mobutu's oldest friends.

But a coup de theatre, if Kabila suddenly decides to pitch up in Lome, was not entirely ruled out. He flew to Goma on Wednesday with aides saying he was heading for an unspecified meeting and would be absent for three days.
Annan reminded the summit not to forget up to 400,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees still stranded in eastern Zaire.
"We must keep human rights issues at the forefront of our considerations," he said, possibly referring to sketchy reports of massacres committed by the rebels.
The Hutus include ex-soldiers who have fought with Zaire's ragged army to try to stem the rebel tide.
More than 1,000 U.S., French and Belgian troops are massed in Congo, ready to evacuate Westerners from Zaire if necessary.
The presidents at the summit were from Burundi, Cameroon, Congo, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kenya, Mauritania, Mozambique, Namibia, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
